After crossing over on a wave of hype, the self-proclaimed saviour of the UK underground wastes his moment on a bloated album of trap, self-aggrandisement and poorly mixed electronics.
Share
"I wanted to claim myself as London's saviour, just to see if anyone would challenge me." When an 18-year-old Vincezio Camille, AKA fakemink, offered this provocation to no bells around the release of his self-produced mixtape, London's Saviour, it sounded like youthful hubris. Three years later, he's been all but vindicated. 

Between mingling with celebs, walking runways and becoming the UK rap underground's leading superstar in the process, his ascent is undeniable. And the hype was well-founded: here was an artist who could go anywhere, pivoting effortlessly from the dense trap of "Music and Me" to the aloof synthpop of "Fever," right through to "Easter Pink," an indie-dance cut tailor-made for a Girls closing credit. But now that his saviour complex is justified, his debut studio LP, Terrified, fails to recapture the dynamic thrill of his early releases. Glimmers of that ingenuity surface, but Camille's head seems stuck in the intoxicating clouds of his newfound fame, leaving the substance far below.

Much of the 19-track record is an exercise in paint-by-numbers, bitcrushed trap that—while not without its charms—quickly becomes monotonous, overbearing and forgettable. Barring the wonderful mess of blasting synths on "Tell Me What You're Missin." and the growling low end on "Wrong Relief," the frenetic pacing of these often sub-three-minute tracks deprives the listening experience of much-needed dynamism. Forgettable cuts like "Rewind" and "Essex Girls" arrive one after another, blurring into an inconsequential mess of bored, reductive raps about his sexual conquests at sluggish tempos. 

Three absurdly aggrandising spoken-word interludes also do significant damage. These overlong poems—which mythologise his journey to fame using heavy-handed religious overtones—eat up more than ten minutes of the hour-long runtime. The effect is like eating a piece of meat braised in its own fat: the first bites might be appetising, but you are ultimately left with indigestion. By the time the album closes, a bloated tracklist stuffed with maximally saturated beats leaves a remarkably dull aftertaste. 

Camille spends much of Terrified dissecting his celebrity status, detailing the constant tension between the terrors of his journey and his long-held desire for stardom. Painting a paranoid picture of vulturous industry politics and soul-sucking fake friends, "All Eyes On Me" is a compelling cry for help. The track lands on a minimal synth line that frays at the seams, projecting a listless nervousness that is mirrored perfectly in his bars. "This town is full of people tryna ruin you / Sometimes I'm sitting, thinking, 'What would Jesus do?'" he raps, hinting at the obsession with grandiosity that consumed him long before he ever tasted fame.

The best moments on Terrified play to Camille's strengths. The title track, an opening instrumental, sounds otherworldly, where an unnerving quasi-techno beat pounds beneath a fiery yet minimal buzz. "Night, Blooming Jasmine" is an obvious standout. He compares himself to the biblical Samson over a beat that chugs slowly below cute synth lines that ebb and flow politely. As he raps, "Killing Charles Manson, ringing for ransom" over what could be mistaken for a "Show Me Love" sample is exactly the kind of preposterous juxtaposition that made him distinct in the first place. But moments like these are fleetingly rare. 

That holier-than-thou shtick felt exciting on the come-up, but now that his eminence has manifested, the navel-gazing has begun to distort his world view. He has the hype, but what of the humility? There's a religious aura surrounding songs like "Rétard Angel," where Camille positions himself as a philosopher-king writing a psalm that comes across as a deeply unempathetic attempt at edginess. It's beholden to the same vapidity as forgiving" fans for disliking his live show and calling himself "one of the most important artists alive right now."

Ultimately, Terrified reveals the truth of Camille's psyche: that beneath the terror, paranoia and growing pains, he has simply drunk his own Kool Aid. Once upon a time, this self-aggrandisement was a tool to wish his stardom into being. Now, it just paints a picture of an artist unable to bridge the gap between his divine aspirations and true inspiration. A waste.
